items.title: 66100_Bud Freeman oral history interview
items.q: I think that I learned more actually from the black dancers and black singers such as Ethel Waters and Bessie Smith than I did from black players

ctx.x: which was the place to be in those days. Because of Chicago supported jazz for a few years, and then of course, when Louis and all the greats left, went east to New York, we followed, because we felt that New York was the place that then could afford to support jazz and one could actually make a living playing music, jazz. There were so many recordings.

Now, to get back to the black business again. I think that I learned more actually from the black dancers and black singers such as Ethel Waters and Bessie Smith than I did from black players, but the strange thing about it all was that I was not influenced by one kind of jazz. For instance, the first time I heard Coleman Hawkins play, I was amazed to hear the powerful authority this man had on the tenor because in those days, tenor was played as an accompanimental instrument. I was supposed to be the first white…

But I would like to think that King Oliver and Louis started the so-called Chicago Jazz. Because what we played on those records was our, the white man's impression, of what King Oliver and Louis were doing.
